read.sections.1.text.back: A budget is a plan about how to use money or time. A budget helps you compare what you have with what you need and want. A budget is not only for money. Mei makes a time budget for her evenings. She sets aside time to help prepare dinner, to rest, and to read English for 15 minutes. Making a budget is really about choices, and every choice has an opportunity cost. If Mei reads for 15 minutes, her time for playing games on the shared phone goes down by 15 minutes. This is a sacrifice (trade-off): giving up one thing to get another. A carefully made budget helps you see your sacrifices before you choose.
read.sections.1.text.source: A budget is a plan for how to use money or time. It helps you compare what you have with what you need and want. Budgets are not only for money. Mei makes a time budget for her evenings. She plans time to help with dinner, to rest and to read English for 15 minutes. Budgeting is really about choices, and every choice has an opportunity cost. If Mei reads for 15 minutes, she has 15 fewer minutes for games on the shared phone. This is a trade-off: giving up one thing to get another. A careful budget helps you see your trade-offs before you choose.

watch.summary.back: This short video for younger learners explains spending and saving. People use money to get things they need and want. But no one can have everything they want. This is called scarcity, so people must choose. Usually people get what they need first, before what they want. For example, the speaker in the video needs a healthy lunch, but wants a cupcake. So lunch comes first. Then the speaker checks whether there is still money left for a cupcake. If you spend, you get something now. But maybe the item is small, and maybe you have little money left. If you save, you have to wait, and that can be hard. But later you can get something more expensive. There is no single most correct answer. Think about the good side and bad side of each choice.
watch.summary.source: This short video for younger learners explains spending and saving. People use money to get the things they need and want. But no one can have everything they want. This is called scarcity, so people must make choices. People usually get what they need before what they want. For example, the speaker needs a healthy lunch but wants a cupcake. So lunch comes first. Then the speaker checks if there is money left for the cupcake. When you spend, you get something now. But it may be small, and you may have little money left. When you save, you have to wait, and that can be hard. But later you can get something that costs more. There is no one right answer. Think about the good and bad sides of each choice.

read.sections.0.heading.back: Spending now and saving for later
read.sections.0.heading.source: Spending now and saving for later

read.sections.0.text.back: Some choices only affect today, but there are also some that affect what we can do later. Spending means using money or other resources to get something now, like food or a bus ride. Spending is not a bad thing, because everyone needs some things now. Saving means keeping some money or resources for later. Saving is hard if we don't have much, but small amounts can add up over time. Sami puts some coins in a tin at home until he has enough money to buy an exercise book. In some communities, neighbours save together in a group. Each person pays a small amount into the group every week, and every week one person takes it all.
read.sections.0.text.source: Some choices affect only today, but others affect what we can do later. To spend means to use money or another resource to get something now, such as food or a bus ride. Spending is not bad, because everyone needs some things now. To save means to keep some money or resources for later. Saving is hard when there is not much, but small amounts can add up over time. Sami puts a few coins in a tin at home until he has enough for a notebook. In some communities, neighbours save together in a group. Each person puts a small amount into the group every week, and each week one person takes it all.

read.sections.0.simpler.back: There are choices for today. There are choices for later. Spending is using money or things now. Everyone needs to spend, for example on food. Saving is keeping money or things for later. Small money becomes a lot over time. Sami puts some coins into a tin. Soon he can buy an exercise book. Some neighbours save together. Each person gives a little money each week. Each week, one person takes it all.

Each person puts in a little every week. Each week, one person takes it all.

read.sections.1.simpler.back: A budget is a plan for your money or time. A budget helps you see what you have and need. Mei makes a time budget for the evening. She helps cook dinner. She rests. She reads English for 15 minutes. So her time for playing games goes down. That is a sacrifice (trade-off). You let go of one thing to get another.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: A budget is a plan for your money or time. It helps you see what you have and what you need. Mei makes a time budget for her evenings. She helps with dinner. She rests. She reads English for 15 minutes. So she has less time for games on the phone. That is a trade-off. You give up one thing to get another.

read.sections.2.text.back: A goal is something you want to do or get, and you work to reach it step by step. No one can control everything about the future, and plans can change when things around us change. That is why small short-term goals are useful. They are goals you can work on now, like learning 10 new English words a week, practising a skill, or looking after your health. A strong plan is also flexible. Mei's Plan A is to read every evening. Her Plan B is to read at lunchtime if the evening is busy. A flexible plan keeps going when life changes.

write.example.back: The goal is that Sami can buy one exercise book and two pens for English class. Every week, he will put half of the coins he gets into a tin at home. He will save these coins and cut down on buying sweets. The sacrifice is fewer sweets now, but an exercise book later. educatorNotes.0.source: The Friday savings group is a rotating savings group. These are found in many parts of the world under local names; the FAO source lists, for example, susu (Ghana), arisan (Indonesia), ekub (Ethiopia) and tontines (West Africa). A partner can use a local name. Present it as something adults organise, based on trust, not as advice for learners to join one.
educatorNotes.0.note: The lesson's 'kelompok tabungan hari Jumat' is an arisan; the note keeps the lesson's words and lists 'arisan' as the Indonesian name, as the English does. Consider whether teachers should be told to call it 'arisan' in class.
educatorNotes.0.back: The Friday savings group is a rotating savings group. Groups like this exist in many parts of the world under local names; the FAO source names, for example, susu (Ghana), arisan (Indonesia), ekub (Ethiopia) and tontine (West Africa). Partners can use the local name. Present this group as something organised by adults and based on trust, not as a suggestion that learners join.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: The lesson avoids pay, bank accounts, loans and long career plans on purpose. Keep discussion to small, short goals that learners can control. Do not ask learners where they will live in future or about their household's money. If a learner finds talk about the future upsetting, return to the small goals in the lesson and do not press.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: This lesson deliberately doesn't cover wages, bank accounts, loans and long-term career plans. Keep discussion to small, short-term goals learners can control. Don't ask learners where they will live in the future or about their household finances. If talk about the future makes a learner anxious, go back to the small goals in the lesson and don't push.
